openers.title: Robot or Person?
openers.prompt: I asked, "What is your favorite food?" One helper said, "Pizza, because my grandma makes it on Fridays!" The other said, "Many people like pizza." Which one was a robot?
openers.teacher: Read both answers twice, then students hold up one finger for the first helper, two for the second, or a fist for not sure. Ask: "What clue helped you decide?"
openers.answer: The second one sounds like a robot. A robot does not eat or have a grandma; it guesses words that often go together.
openers.lookFor: Students name a clue, such as "robots don't eat" or "the first one told a real memory."
openers.next: Tomorrow we will train our own pretend robot and see how it makes guesses.

openers.title: What Will Robot Guess?
openers.prompt: Our pretend robot only ever saw red apples. Now it sees a green apple. What will it guess, and why?
openers.teacher: Partners turn knee to knee and each share a guess and a reason. Call on three pairs, then ask: "How could we help the robot guess better next time?"
openers.answer: The robot might say "not an apple" because it learned that apples are red. Robots guess from the patterns they have seen, so showing it more kinds of apples helps.
openers.lookFor: Students say the robot learned from what it saw, and suggest showing it more kinds of apples.
openers.next: Tonight, find something at home that comes in many colors and tell a grown-up why a robot might get confused.

openers.title: Robot Says: Check It!
openers.prompt: A robot helper said, "Cats have wings and can fly to the moon!" Is that a fact or fake?
openers.teacher: Students show thumbs up for fact or thumbs down for fake, then name two places they could check (a book, a grown-up, a trusted website). Optional: you type a simple question into a district-approved chatbot on the projector and the class checks its answer in a book.
openers.answer: Fake. Robot helpers can sound very sure and still be wrong, so we check in two places before we believe them.
openers.lookFor: Students name two ways to check, like "look in a cat book" and "ask my teacher."
openers.next: When a helper tells you something new today, ask yourself, "Where else can I check?"

openers.title: Secret or Share?
openers.prompt: A game asks you some questions. Which ones are OK to share, and which ones stay secret?
openers.teacher: Read each item; students pat their head for "OK to share" or put a finger on their lips for "keep it secret." Ask: "If a game or a talking computer asks for a secret, who do you tell?"
openers.answer: Favorite color and a pet's trick are OK. Address, password, full name, and school stay private, and you tell a trusted grown-up if anything asks for them.
openers.lookFor: Students keep address, password, and school private and name a trusted grown-up they would tell.
openers.next: Tonight, ask a grown-up at home which things in our family stay private online.

openers.title: Kind Click Thumbs
openers.prompt: Tomás sends a message: "Your drawing is SO cool!" Then Pip sends: "Your drawing is ugly." Which one is a kind click?
openers.teacher: Read each message separately; students give thumbs up or down. Then pairs turn Pip's message into a kind one, and ask: "What should you do if someone sends you an unkind message?"
openers.lookFor: Pairs change Pip's words into something kind, and students say they would tell a trusted grown-up about mean messages.
openers.next: Try one kind click today: say something kind to a friend about their work.

openers.title: Rainbow Wing Dog
openers.prompt: Picture a puppy with rainbow wings flying over a school. Is it real, pretend on purpose, or changed to look real?
openers.teacher: Describe the picture aloud, or show a teacher-made drawing on the projector. Students stand still for real, wiggle for pretend, or freeze like a statue for changed, and then you ask: "What clue did you use, and who could you ask if you weren't sure?"
openers.answer: Puppies do not have wings, so it is pretend or changed. A cartoon is pretend on purpose; a photo made to look real is changed, and a grown-up can help you tell.
openers.lookFor: Students give a clue, such as "dogs don't have wings," and name a grown-up to ask.
openers.next: Look at one picture at home tonight and ask, "Is it real, pretend, or changed?"

openers.title: Who Made It? Why?
openers.prompt: A cartoon tiger on a cereal box says, "Eat Zoomy O's every day!" Who made that tiger, and why?
openers.teacher: Partners take turns saying "I think ___ made it because ___." Share a few, then ask: "Is the tiger helping you or selling to you?"
openers.answer: The cereal company made the tiger to get people to buy Zoomy O's. Every picture and video was made by someone for a reason.
openers.lookFor: Students use "because" and name a reason, such as "so we buy the cereal."
openers.next: Tonight, find one picture or logo at home and ask a grown-up, "Who made this, and why?"

openers.title: Move or Sit?
openers.prompt: I will say things kids like to do. Stand up if it moves your body. Sit down if you sit still.
openers.teacher: Call out each activity and let students stand or sit. Then ask: "How does your body feel after moving? After sitting a long time?"
openers.lookFor: Students name a feeling, such as "wiggly" or "happy," and say screens are OK when we also move.
openers.next: Tonight, choose one moving activity to do with your family.

openers.title: Speaker or Grown-Up?
openers.prompt: A talking speaker can help with some things. For which ones should you ask a grown-up instead?
options: Is this berry safe to eat?
openers.teacher: Read each one; students point to the ceiling for "speaker can help" or to you for "ask a grown-up." Ask: "Why is a grown-up better for some questions?"
openers.answer: Songs, timers, and weather are fine for a speaker. Getting hurt or eating berries needs a grown-up, because the speaker only guesses and cannot see you.
openers.lookFor: Students say a speaker "can't see you" or "might guess wrong" for the safety questions.
openers.next: Talk with your family about what your home helpers can and cannot do.

openers.title: Draw a Helper Bot
openers.prompt: Pretend a robot helper comes to our class someday. Draw one helpful thing it does, and one rule it must follow.
openers.teacher: Students draw on scrap paper or whiteboards for five minutes, then share with a neighbor. Ask: "Why does your robot need that rule?"
openers.lookFor: Each drawing shows a helpful job and a rule, such as "no taking pictures without asking."
openers.next: We will vote on one class rule for helper robots and post it on our wall.

openers.title: Team Drawing Choice
openers.prompt: Our class is making a picture of our school garden. Would you rather each draw alone, or all add to one big drawing together?
openers.teacher: Students walk to one side of the room for each choice. Each side shares one reason, then ask: "How could we use both ideas?"
openers.lookFor: Students listen to the other side and suggest a mix, such as "draw alone, then glue them together."
openers.next: Today during centers, share one idea with a partner before you start working.

openers.title: Password Keepers
openers.prompt: A password is like a toothbrush: it's just for you. Stand up if it's OK to share your password with this person.
openers.teacher: Call out each one; students stand or stay seated. Ask: "Why is it OK for your grown-up to know it, but not your best friend?"
openers.answer: Only your grown-ups at home and your teacher (for school logins) should know it. Friends, game characters, and people in videos do not get your password.
openers.lookFor: Students stay seated for friends and game characters and explain that grown-ups help keep them safe.
openers.next: Ask your grown-up tonight who helps keep your passwords safe at home.

openers.title: You Won a Prize?
openers.prompt: You are playing a game and a box pops up: "You won a prize! Tap here!" What do you do?
openers.teacher: Partners act it out: one reads the pop-up, the other shows what they would do. Ask: "Who is your trusted grown-up for moments like this?"
openers.answer: Don't tap it. Stop, and show a trusted grown-up. Surprise prizes online are often tricks.
openers.lookFor: Students say "stop and tell a grown-up" instead of "tap it."
openers.next: Tell a grown-up at home our rule: stop and show before you tap.

openers.title: Super-Speed Cereal?
openers.prompt: A cartoon bunny says, "Crunchy Stars cereal makes you run faster than a car!" Fact or fake?
openers.teacher: Students show thumbs up or down, then tell a partner why. Optional: show a teacher-made ad drawing on the projector. Ask: "Is the bunny telling you something or selling you something?"
openers.answer: Fake. It is an ad, and ads try to get you to buy. No cereal makes you run faster than a car.
openers.lookFor: Students use the words "ad" or "selling" when explaining their thumb.
openers.next: Count the ads you notice at home tonight and share one tomorrow.

openers.title: Say Whose Idea
openers.prompt: Mia drew a cat. Leo put Mia's cat on the class board and said, "Look what I made!" Was that fair?
openers.teacher: Students show thumbs up for fair or down for not fair. Then pairs practice what Leo could say instead, and ask: "How would Mia feel?"
openers.answer: Not fair. Leo should say, "Mia made this." We always say whose idea or picture it is, even if a computer helped.
openers.lookFor: Pairs practice a sentence like "Mia drew this cat."
openers.next: When you share work today, say who helped you.
